analysis.one_liner: Creates a public Medicare-based health plan anyone could buy, and lets the government negotiate drug prices.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees in October 2017 and never advanced; no committee or floor vote was ever taken before Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a new government-run health plan, called the Medicare Exchange health plan, that anyone buying insurance on the individual or small-group markets could choose instead of a private plan. It would have started in areas with little or no competition, expanded everywhere by 2023, and paid doctors and hospitals at Medicare rates, which are usually lower than what private insurers pay — so its premiums could be cheaper. The bill also would have repealed the legal ban on the government negotiating prescription drug prices for Medicare. It never received a single vote in either chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: People buying their own or small-business health insurance — especially in rural areas and places where only one insurer offers plans — would gain a lower-cost public option. Medicare beneficiaries would also gain if negotiated drug prices lowered what they pay. Anyone dissatisfied with private insurer premiums and networks would have a new alternative.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People buying individual and small-group coverage

how_it_helps.text: Creates a public Medicare-based plan in the individual and small-group insurance markets, giving residents of every state a government-backed option to buy, starting first in areas with little insurer competition or provider shortages.
Reimburses doctors and hospitals at Medicare rates, which are typically lower than private-insurer rates, so the plan's premiums can be set below what private plans charge.
Removes the legal restriction that currently bars the government from negotiating prescription drug prices for Medicare, allowing the Secretary to negotiate drug prices, including for Part D drugs.

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers would lose customers to a cheaper government plan, and would face price pressure. Hospitals and doctors would be paid Medicare rates — generally lower than private rates — for the new plan's patients. Pharmaceutical companies would lose the legal protection that blocks Medicare drug-price negotiation. Taxpayers would fund the plan's $1 billion startup reserve fund.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private insurers, hospitals, and drug makers

drawbacks.text: Starting the plan first in areas with one insurer or provider shortages could destabilize fragile insurance markets in rural and low-competition areas, if private plans exit in response to a cheaper public competitor.

The plan relies on $1 billion in startup funding plus administrative appropriations, and its premiums were required to cover full actuarial cost, so if enrollment skews sicker or costlier than expected, taxpayers could be on the hook beyond projections.
Hospitals and physicians could see revenue pressure from Medicare-rate reimbursement, which critics argued could reduce access in areas where private plans already pay above Medicare rates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential gains for consumers were substantial: a cheaper public plan could pressure private insurers to lower premiums, and drug negotiation could cut prices for seniors. The costs were real but speculative — startup funding of $1 billion [S3], uncertainty about whether Medicare rates are adequate everywhere, and provider concerns that government-set rates would reduce payments. The main flaw was political, not design: it was introduced without a realistic path forward in a Congress that took no action on it, so the trade-off was never actually weighed by lawmakers.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees and their health subcommittee, and none of them ever acted on it before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The Medicare-X Choice Act was introduced in the House on October 23, 2017 by Rep. Brian Higgins with nine Democratic cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, then to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health on October 27, 2017.
No committee ever reported the bill, no floor vote was scheduled, and the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, killing the bill.
The bill would have created a Medicare-based public plan in the individual and small-group markets and removed the legal bar on government negotiation of Medicare drug prices.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private insurers and pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would have faced a low-cost public competitor and government drug-price negotiation, are better off because the bill never moved.

for.name: Reps. Larson, Courtney, Scott (VA), O'Rourke, and Polis
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and its health subcommittee took no action; no markup or vote was ever held.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and took no action on it.

against.name: Private health insurance and pharmaceutical industries
against.what_they_did: Consistently opposed public-option proposals during this period as competitors to private coverage; their influence over the committees of jurisdiction is widely reported.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all nine cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and the Democratic-controlled committees never acted on it.

industries.note: A government-run plan paying Medicare rates would compete directly with private exchange plans on price, threatening their enrollment and margins in individual and small-group markets. This competition is the bill's core purpose.
Eliminating the anti-negotiation restriction would let Medicare negotiate drug prices directly, ending a provision that has shielded drug makers from price negotiation since 2003.

Providers would automatically become participating providers in the new plan but would be paid at Medicare rates, which are generally lower than private rates, though they gain access to a large new pool of enrollees.
